chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Critics as parasites: George Frazier and the Tilton insult
summary: Wilson says Frazier made his name by calling Goodman's singer Martha Tilton bad, then left jazz writing.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Some of the writers, I remember,

George Frazier busted into the jazz world years ago and created a big niche for himself by coming out in some important jazz publication by saying Martha Tilton stinks. When Benny Goodman was on top, after the '38 concert, with Nancy Tilton singing, and here's an unknown writer coming up saying that the most popular girl singer, the most popular jazz band stinks, in his words.

So what does he do? He goes and gets a job with one of these daily papers in Boston and he never wrote another word about jazz -- making a lot of money writing about other stuff. Unfortunately, he died writing for this paper in Boston.*

But those people used jazz, and those are the parasites, and that's a cynical way to break into the field, by criticizing a big name singer and saying she stinks. But that is cynical, like the Ayatollah, he doesn't care whose head rolls, or like Hitler did, that kind of mentality. So many in the jazz world are not sincere, associated with the jazz movement. They don't respect jazz musicians. A lot of these guys come around simpering and smiling, with their little pencils and papers, people with the magazines, and looking up the jazz musician.
